paper_a.title: A Differential Equation for Modeling Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method: Theory and Insights

paper_b.title: Some Methods of Speeding Up the Convergence of Iteration Methods

metadata.description: Su-Boyd-Candes (2014) extends Polyak's (1964) heavy-ball framework: Polyak introduced both the discrete two-step momentum iteration $x^{n+1}=x^n-\alpha P(x^n)+\beta(x^n-x^{n-1})$ and its continuous analogue $\ddot x = \alpha_2 \dot x + \alpha_1 P(x)$, proved local convergence with rate $(\sqrt M-\sqrt m)/(\sqrt M+\sqrt m)$ for strongly convex quadratics, and developed a general $k$-step iteration / $k$-th order ODE theory. Su-Boyd-Candes derive the time-varying-damping ODE $\ddot X+(3/t)\dot X+\nabla f(X)=0$ as the continuous limit of Nesterov's accelerated method, establish $O(1/t^2)$ on convex (not just strongly convex) $f$ via a Lyapunov energy, generalize to damping $r/t$, and extend to composite/non-smooth and strongly-convex regimes with restarting. The two papers thus instantiate the same conceptual programme — second-order momentum ODEs as a tool for analysing accelerated first-order methods — with Su-Boyd-Candes deepening it for the Nesterov branch. Paper B is PDF-fallback (1964 classic), so node names/types are weighted over LaTeX fidelity.

matches.explanation: Both state the basic optimization problem: minimize a (smooth/differentiable) convex functional. Polyak phrases it in Hilbert space and reduces to $\nabla f(x)=0$; Su-Boyd-Candes phrase it in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Same mathematical object.

Polyak's general operator equation $P(x)=0$ (root-finding in a Banach space, possibly nonlinear) is the analogue of Su-Boyd-Candes's composite $f=g+h$ minimization through the gradient/subgradient: Polyak recovers optimization as the special case $P=\nabla f$. Polyak is more general (root-finding); SBC is more specialized (composite convex), so the match is conceptual rather than identical.

The class $\mathcal{F}_L$ of $L$-smooth convex functions (and its union $\mathcal{F}_\infty$) is a Su-Boyd-Candes setting; Polyak instead works in Banach/Hilbert spaces with operator-theoretic spectral hypotheses ($m\le A\le M$) and does not isolate an $\mathcal{F}_L$ class.

Strong convexity class $\mathcal{S}_\mu$ is named/defined explicitly in SBC; Polyak uses the equivalent operator-spectrum condition $m(y,y)\le(Ay,y)\le M(y,y)$ inside Theorem 9 (TP256.9) without naming a class. The condition itself is captured by TP256.9's assumptions, not by a separate definition node.
Proximal subgradient $G_s$ and directional subgradient $G(x,p;f)$ are SBC machinery for composite/non-smooth extension; Polyak's framework is purely smooth/operator-theoretic and has no counterpart.
Speed restarting time is an SBC innovation (2014). Polyak does not consider restarting schemes.

Both are two-step / momentum first-order methods for convex minimization. Polyak's heavy-ball $x^{n+1}=x^n-\alpha P(x^n)+\beta(x^n-x^{n-1})$ uses a constant momentum coefficient $\beta$; Nesterov's scheme uses time-varying $(k-1)/(k+2)$ (or $(k-1)/(k+r-1)$ in the generalized version). They are different methods in the same family — both yield the optimal $(\sqrt M-\sqrt m)/(\sqrt M+\sqrt m)$-style rate on strongly convex quadratics — and both papers explicitly cast them as discretizations of a second-order ODE.
Speed-restarting Nesterov is a contribution unique to SBC. Polyak's heavy-ball is run with fixed parameters; restarting did not appear in 1964.

Forward-Euler discretization of the smoothed ODE is an SBC analytical device; Polyak does not discretize his continuous analogue (he treats discrete and continuous methods in parallel, not as discretizations of one another).

Polyak gives an explicit empirical parameter-tuning protocol for $\alpha,\beta$ (start with $\beta=0$, raise to $0.8$-$0.99$ when convergence slows, double $\alpha$, etc.); SBC has no comparable practical heuristic node.

Both are second-order momentum ODEs of the form $\ddot X + (\text{damping})\,\dot X + \nabla f(X) = 0$. Polyak's continuous heavy-ball $\ddot x = \alpha_2 \dot x + \alpha_1 P(x)$ has constant damping $\alpha_2$ and a sign convention $\alpha_2,\alpha_1<0$; SBC introduce time-varying damping $3/t$ (or $r/t$). Su-Boyd-Candes Remark RP255.2 (time invariance) explicitly singles out the $C/t$ form, distinguishing their ODE from Polyak's constant-damping case — this is the principal mathematical novelty of SBC and the core of the EXT relationship.

EP256.3 is the discrete heavy-ball iteration $x^{n+1}=x^n-\alpha P(x^n)+\beta(x^n-x^{n-1})$ — the equation form of Polyak's two-step method. SBC's Nesterov scheme AP255.1 and the generalized scheme AP255.2 are the analogous discrete momentum recursions, with the sole difference being the time-varying $(k-1)/(k+r-1)$ momentum coefficient in place of Polyak's constant $\beta$. Listed separately from the algorithm-level match above because the equation node and algorithm node carry different metadata in the source JSONs.

Polyak's linear operator equation $Ax=b$ is the special case of his framework that Theorems 3-4 (TP256.3-4) target. SBC do not address linear systems specifically — their setting is convex minimization (smooth or composite), so this Polyak problem has no SBC counterpart.
Smoothed ODE with $3/\max(\delta,t)$ is a technical regularization for SBC's existence proof; no Polyak counterpart.
Speed-restarted ODE has no counterpart in Polyak.
Composite-optimization ODE with directional subgradient $G$ has no counterpart in Polyak's smooth setup.
Polyak's general $k$-step linear recurrence and $k$-th order ODE are introduced as a unifying framework that contains the heavy-ball case ($k=2$); SBC do not consider general $k$-step schemes.

Polyak's general definitions of $k$-step iteration method and operational matrix / determinant on $B^k$ are the linear-algebraic backbone of his theorems; SBC have no analogue (they handle only the second-order case directly).

Polyak's spectrum-of-commuting-operators lemmas (LP256.1-5), spectral-radius/exponential bounds (LP256.6-7), companion-matrix convergence lemmas (LP256.8-9), and nonlinear-perturbation lemmas (LP256.10-11) build the operational-matrix machinery for his $k$-step theory. SBC's analysis is via Lyapunov / energy methods on a single second-order ODE; none of these spectral lemmas have a counterpart.

Polyak's general convergence theorems for linear $k$-step iterations and $k$-th order ODEs (rates governed by the spectral hypothesis on the characteristic polynomial $\mu^k=\sum f_i(\lambda)\mu^{k-i}$) are the abstract framework of his paper. SBC do not establish a comparable general $k$-step result.
Polyak's $k$-step theorems specialised to the linear equation $Ax=b$. SBC do not address linear systems specifically.

Polyak's nonlinear-perturbation $k$-step convergence theorems for $P(x)=0$. The local-convergence-from-spectral-condition pattern is generic; SBC's strongly-convex theorem TP255.8 / TP255.10 are the closest in spirit but use a Lyapunov rather than spectral approach, so we keep these unmatched.

Existence/uniqueness of the $3/t$-damped ODE with singular drift at $t=0$ is an SBC-specific technical theorem; Polyak's continuous existence (LP256.9) is for constant-coefficient linear systems and does not need this kind of argument.

Convergence-of-Nesterov-iterates-to-the-ODE (the discrete-to-continuous limit) is the central SBC contribution. Polyak does not formulate his discrete iteration as a discretization of his ODE — the two are studied in parallel via the same spectral framework — so there is no analogue.

$O(1/t^2)$ rate of the SBC ODE on plain convex $f$ (and its $r$-generalization) is the headline SBC result. Polyak's continuous theorems (TP256.2/TP256.4/TP256.8) establish only exponential rates under spectral hypotheses that imply strong convexity; the polynomial-rate-on-merely-convex result has no Polyak counterpart.

Oscillation-roots theorem for strongly convex 1D $f$ describes phase behaviour of the SBC ODE; Polyak's results (e.g. RP255.6 in SBC, the Bessel-function representation) and his rates do not include this kind of root-spacing analysis.

Discrete high-friction $O(1/k^2)$ rate for the generalized Nesterov scheme. Polyak's discrete heavy-ball rate TP256.9 part (3) gives only the strongly-convex rate, not an $O(1/k^2)$ bound on plain convex $f$.
Low-friction $r<3$ result under convexity of $(f-f^\star)^{(r-1)/2}$ is SBC-specific.

$O(t^{-\alpha})$ continuous rate for strongly convex $f$ (SBC). Polyak's continuous result TP256.9(5) gives an exponential rate $r_2$ for the strongly-convex continuous heavy-ball, which is qualitatively different (exponential vs polynomial-with-tunable-exponent), so we do not pair them.
$O(1/k^3)$ rate for generalized Nesterov on strongly convex $f$ is a sharper-than-Polyak SBC result; Polyak gives only the $\bar q_2$ geometric rate.

Both establish linear (geometric / exponential) convergence on strongly convex $f$ via a momentum method. Polyak (TP256.9) gives the classical local rate $\bar q_2 = (\sqrt M-\sqrt m)/(\sqrt M+\sqrt m)$ for the discrete heavy-ball and the explicit exponential rate $r_2 = (\alpha_2+\sqrt g)/2$ for the continuous heavy-ball; SBC (TP255.10) gives a linear rate $e^{-c_2 t\sqrt L}$ for the *speed-restarted* ODE, with constants depending only on the condition number $L/\mu$. Same conceptual pay-off (linear rate on strongly convex via momentum) achieved through fundamentally different mechanisms (constant-damping ODE vs. time-varying-damping ODE plus restarts).
Composite-ODE rate (with directional subgradient) is SBC's non-smooth extension; no Polyak analogue.

Cluster of SBC technical lemmas: smoothed-ODE uniform bounds (LP255.2-5), Arzelà-Ascoli existence (LP255.1), local uniqueness via Gronwall (LP255.6-7), Euler-vs-Nesterov error (LP255.8), and speed-restarting bounds (LP255.10-13). All are tied to the singular $3/t$ damping or to the restarting analysis, so they have no Polyak counterpart. Polyak's analogue lemmas (LP256.*) likewise have no SBC counterpart, listed separately above.
Proofs of SBC theorems with no Polyak analogue (existence, Nesterov-to-ODE limit, discrete and inductive higher-order rates, restart linear-rate, composite ODE).

PP255.3 / PP255.4 prove SBC's continuous $O(1/t^2)$ via a Lyapunov energy $\mathcal{E}(t) = t^2(f(X)-f^\star) + 2\|X+t\dot X/2 - x^\star\|^2$ (and its $r$-generalisation). Polyak's PP256.15 proves the heavy-ball convergence by analysing roots of the characteristic quadratic $\mu^2 - (1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)\mu - \beta = 0$ inside his general $k$-step framework. Same target (rate of a momentum method on convex $f$) but fundamentally different proof technique — Lyapunov vs. spectral. Marked analogous because both are the central convergence proofs of their respective momentum methods.
Polyak's spectral / operational-matrix proofs (LP256.1-7, TP256.1-8) have no analogue in SBC's Lyapunov-based programme.

Both papers close with open problems about extending the local/asymptotic theory. SBC asks for a provable linear rate for gradient restarting (OpenP255.1) and a general ODE-to-discrete translation theory (OpenP255.2). Polyak asks for nonlocal convergence theorems for nonlinear multistep methods (OpenP256.1) and for nonlinear/nonstationary multistep schemes (OpenP256.2). Conceptually overlapping (both seek to push beyond local/linear analyses of momentum-type methods) but the specific technical questions differ; grouped in one composite analogous match.
